claim_verdicts.evidence: RFC 9110 §15: "The first digit of the status code defines the class of response. The last two digits do not have any categorization role. There are five values for the first digit", then the list 1xx (Informational), 2xx (Successful), 3xx (Redirection), 4xx (Client Error), 5xx (Server Error). §15.2: "The 1xx (Informational) class of status code indicates an interim response for communicating connection status or request progress prior to completing the requested action and sending a final response."

RFC 9110 §15: "a client MUST understand the class of any status code, as indicated by the first digit, and treat an unrecognized status code as being equivalent to the x00 status code of that class", with the worked example "if a client receives an unrecognized status code of 471, it can see from the first digit that there was something wrong with its request and treat the response as if it had received a 400 (Bad Request)". The lesson's "must fall back to the first digit" carries the same MUST.

RFC 9110 §15.3.1: "The 200 (OK) status code indicates that the request has succeeded. The content sent in a 200 response depends on the request method." The per-method table gives, for GET, response content that is a representation of "the target resource". The claim and the lesson both restrict the body half to GET.

RFC 9110 §15.3.2: "The 201 (Created) status code indicates that the request has been fulfilled and has resulted in one or more new resources being created." The claim asserts exactly that; it does not make Location mandatory, which matches the RFC (the created resource may instead be identified by the target URI).

RFC 9110 §15.3.5: "The 204 (No Content) status code indicates that the server has successfully fulfilled the request and that there is no additional content to send in the response content." §6.4.1: "All 1xx (Informational), 204 (No Content), and 304 (Not Modified) responses do not include content." Both halves of the claim are covered.

RFC 9110 §15.4.2: "The 301 (Moved Permanently) status code indicates that the target resource has been assigned a new permanent URI"; §15.4.3: "The 302 (Found) status code indicates that the target resource resides temporarily under a different URI." Each section then says "The server SHOULD generate a Location header field in the response". The claim's "expected (SHOULD)" matches that requirement level; the lesson's "both expected to name the new address in Location" does not overstate it as MUST.

RFC 9110 §15.4.5 makes the answer conditional on the request: "The 304 (Not Modified) status code indicates that a conditional GET or HEAD request has been received and would have resulted in a 200 (OK) response if it were not for the fact that the condition evaluated to false ... the client, which made the request conditional, already has a valid representation". Both the claim and the lesson state the consequence without the precondition, so a reader may expect a 304 for a plain GET. The no-body half is right (§6.4.1).
claim_verdicts.suggested_text: 304 answers a conditional request: it tells the client that the copy it already holds is still usable, and the response carries no body.

claim_verdicts.evidence: RFC 9110 §15.5.1, word for word: "The 400 (Bad Request) status code indicates that the server cannot or will not process the request due to something that is perceived to be a client error". §15.5.2: 401 means the request "has not been applied because it lacks valid authentication credentials for the target resource"; "lacks an identity the server accepts" is a faithful, weaker paraphrase. The same section's WWW-Authenticate MUST is omitted, not contradicted — see the section 5 issue about the lab's own 401.

RFC 9110 §15.5.4: "The 403 (Forbidden) status code indicates that the server understood the request but refuses to fulfill it." §15.5.5: 404 "indicates that the origin server did not find a current representation for the target resource or is not willing to disclose that one exists." §15.5.10: 409 "indicates that the request could not be completed due to a conflict with the current state of the target resource."

RFC 9110 §15.6.1: 500 means "the server encountered an unexpected condition that prevented it from fulfilling the request". §15.6.3: 502 means "the server, while acting as a gateway or proxy, received an invalid response from an inbound server it accessed while attempting to fulfill the request". §15.6.4: 503 means "the server is currently unable to handle the request due to a temporary overload or scheduled maintenance"; the lesson's "not taking work at the moment" stays inside that.

RFC 9110 §15.1: "The reason phrases listed here are only recommendations -- they can be replaced by local equivalents or left out altogether without affecting the protocol." §6.2: "Response message control data includes a status code, optional reason phrase, and protocol version. In HTTP/1.1 and earlier, control data is sent as the first line of a message." RFC 9112 §4 corroborates: "A client SHOULD ignore the reason-phrase content because it is not a reliable channel for information".

RFC 9110 §15.5.4, last paragraph: "An origin server that wishes to 'hide' the current existence of a forbidden target resource MAY instead respond with a status code of 404 (Not Found)." The lesson's "a deliberate choice, not a mistake" matches that MAY; the RFC grants it to an origin server, the lesson says "a server", which is looser but not false for the case it describes.

RFC 9110 §15.5.2 supports the 401 half: the request "lacks valid authentication credentials" and "The user agent MAY repeat the request with a new or replaced Authorization header field". §15.5.4 is weaker than the claim: "If authentication credentials were provided ... the server considers them insufficient to grant access. The client SHOULD NOT automatically repeat the request with the same credentials ... However, a request might be forbidden for reasons unrelated to the credentials." So "changes nothing" is a guarantee the RFC does not give.
claim_verdicts.suggested_text: 401 says the request carries no credentials the server accepts, so sending ones it does accept may change the answer; 403 says the server has already refused, and a client should not automatically repeat the request with the same credentials — a 403 can also be for reasons unrelated to them.

claim_verdicts.evidence: git show stage-0:Caddyfile — @missingOrder path /api/v1/orders/999 -> respond 404; handle /redirect { redir * /index.html 302 }; handle /conflict -> 409; handle /slow -> 503; handle /admin -> 401 with no cookie; final handle -> file_server, so /index.html is 200 and /no-such-page is 404. git show stage-0:outputs/stage-0/scripts/http/status-codes.txt lines 1-7: "200  /index.html", "302  /redirect", "404  /api/v1/orders/999", "401  /admin", "409  /conflict", "503  /slow", "404  /no-such-page".

Caddyfile at stage-0: "handle /redirect { redir * /index.html 302 }". The captured run prints "HTTP/1.1 302 Found" then "Location: /index.html". RFC 9110 §15.4.3 supports the second half: the server's "response content usually contains a short hypertext note with a hyperlink to the different URI(s)", so a client that ignores Location has nothing useful left.

Caddyfile at stage-0: "@guest header Cookie *role=guest*" and handle /admin { route { respond @guest ... 403; respond @signedIn ... 200; respond ... 401 } } — with no Cookie neither matcher fires, so the unconditional 401 answers. The captured run confirms: "  no cookie          401" and "  cookie role=guest  403".

Settled by execution, not by a manual: curl is not a key in content/versions.yaml, so curl.se is not an admissible source, and the sandbox refused to run curl here. Line 8 of the script is the only source of the first seven output lines — curl -sS -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}  $path\n" — and the captured run prints for each path exactly the code the Caddyfile answers with, cross-checked by the status lines dumped later in the same run ("HTTP/1.1 302 Found" for /redirect, "HTTP/1.1 503 Service Unavailable" for /slow).

Execution evidence. Lines 13 and 23 run curl -sS -D - -o /dev/null piped into grep, and the capture holds only header lines: "HTTP/1.1 302 Found", "Location: /index.html", "HTTP/1.1 503 Service Unavailable". None of the bodies the Caddyfile sends for those paths appears anywhere in the capture ("Service Unavailable: the lab is pretending to be overloaded" is never printed). So -D - put header lines on stdout and -o /dev/null discarded the body.

Line 5 of the script is [ -f /.dockerenv ] || exec "$(dirname "$0")/../lab-run.sh" "$0" "$@". scripts/lab-run.sh at stage-0 ends with: exec docker compose exec -T lab bash -c 'exec bash "$0" "$@" 2>&1' "/repo/$rel" "$@", under the comment "run one of this repository's scripts inside the lab box so that its output is the same on Windows, macOS, Linux and CI". docker-compose.yml puts the web service on network_mode "service:lab", so localhost:8080 inside that box is Caddy.
claim_verdicts.source: examples/don-hang scripts/http/status-codes.sh:5; scripts/lab-run.sh; docker-compose.yml at stage-0

claim_verdicts.evidence: RFC 9110 §15: "The status code of a response is a three-digit integer code that describes the result of the request and the semantics of the response, including whether the request was successful and what content is enclosed (if any)." The responder generates that code; the specification defines no rule deriving it from the content. §15.3.1: 200 "indicates that the request has succeeded", so a 200 over a failed operation contradicts the code's meaning while breaking no stated requirement on the sender.

Half is settled by execution: scripts/capture-output.sh runs "bash $script" from the host for every script mentioning lab-run.sh, so at capture time /.dockerenv was absent, line 5's test exited non-zero, and the run still produced the complete 18-line capture (capture-output.sh aborts loudly on a non-zero exit) — set -e did not fire on the left operand of ||. The rest is not settled: bash is not a versions.yaml key and no bash manual is in refs/; the sandbox refused bash -c and any curl probe, and no capture shows a failed connection.
claim_verdicts.source: examples/don-hang scripts/capture-output.sh at stage-0; outputs/stage-0/scripts/http/status-codes.txt; attempted and blocked: bash -c 'set -e' probe, curl against a closed port

claim_verdicts.evidence: RFC 9110 §15.6.3 defines 502 only for "the server, while acting as a gateway or proxy" that "received an invalid response from an inbound server it accessed" — the code is about the answer the intermediary got, which is why what stands behind it is looked at first. §15.6.4 defines 503 with no intermediary at all ("a temporary overload or scheduled maintenance"), so any server can send one on its own account; the lab's 503 for /slow comes straight from Caddy, which has nothing behind it at stage-0. The lesson states both under a condition.
claim_verdicts.source: refs/rfc/rfc9110.txt:7882-7885 (§15.6.3); 7888-7897 (§15.6.4); examples/don-hang Caddyfile at stage-0, handle /slow

claim_verdicts.evidence: RFC 9110 §15: "The status code of a response is a three-digit integer code that describes the result of the request" — a status code exists only inside a response. §15.5.5: 404 "indicates that the origin server did not find a current representation for the target resource or is not willing to disclose that one exists", which presupposes a server that received the request and answered it. A host that never answers leaves no status line to read.

RFC 9110 §15.5: "The 4xx (Client Error) class of status code indicates that the client seems to have erred" — the claim keeps that hedge. §15.5.9 on 408: "If the client has an outstanding request in transit, it MAY repeat that request." §15.5.10 on 409: "This code is used in situations where the user might be able to resolve the conflict and resubmit the request." Neither the class nor those codes forbids a retry, so the lesson's "usually will not help" is the right strength.

RFC 9110 §15.4 states the class as "further action needs to be taken by the user agent in order to fulfill the request" and enumerates the types: "1. Redirects that indicate this resource might be available at a different URI, as provided by the Location header field, as in the status codes 301 (Moved Permanently), 302 (Found)" and "4. Redirection to a previously stored result, as in the 304 (Not Modified) status code." So not every 3xx names another address, exactly as claimed.

issues.quote: `2xx` done, `3xx` elsewhere, `4xx` your request, `5xx` the server
issues.text: Summary line 1 compresses 3xx to "elsewhere", which the lesson body itself refuses to do: section 4 says "the answer is not here as sent — usually somewhere else" and claim 25 says a 304 points at nothing elsewhere (RFC 9110 §15.4 type 4, "Redirection to a previously stored result"). The five-line summary is what the stage gate bank is built from, so this wording travels further than the body.
issues.fix: In summary line 1 replace "`3xx` elsewhere" with "`3xx` not what you asked for", the wording the diagram and quiz q1's explanation already use. Word-neutral: three words for four.

issues.quote: `304` says nothing has changed, so reuse the copy you already hold and read no body
issues.text: A 304 is not an answer a server may give to any GET. RFC 9110 §15.4.5: "The 304 (Not Modified) status code indicates that a conditional GET or HEAD request has been received and would have resulted in a 200 (OK) response if it were not for the fact that the condition evaluated to false". As written, a reader can expect a 304 for a plain GET of an unchanged page. Claim 7 omits the same precondition.
issues.fix: Write "`304` answers a conditional ask with 'nothing has changed', so reuse the copy you already hold and read no body", and update claim 7 to the suggested_text in its verdict. Costs two words; take them from section 5's "the prepared machine the example repository starts for you".

issues.quote: `403` says it has already decided and the answer is still no, so sending the same thing again changes nothing
issues.text: "Changes nothing" is a guarantee RFC 9110 §15.5.4 does not give: it says "The client SHOULD NOT automatically repeat the request with the same credentials" and adds "However, a request might be forbidden for reasons unrelated to the credentials." The lab's own 403 is static, so section 5's version of the sentence is fine; this one generalises it into a rule.
issues.fix: Replace with "`403` says it has already decided, so a client should not keep repeating the request with the same identity". Same length, and it keeps the sign-in-loop point that follows.

issues.quote: `curl` never gets an answer, reports the failed connection, and `set -euo pipefail` on the third line … ends the run at the first address
issues.text: Those mechanics hold only if Caddy alone is stopped. The repo's off-switch is scripts/down.sh ("docker compose down --volumes --remove-orphans"), the counterpart of the scripts/up.sh named one line earlier in Try it, and it removes the `lab` container too; the run then dies inside lab-run.sh at `docker compose exec -T lab`, before any curl runs. Claim 21 carries the same assumption, and its curl half could not be verified here.
issues.fix: Write "With the site switched off but the lab box still running, `curl` never gets an answer …"; stopping the whole lab is a different failure that never reaches the first request.

issues.quote: with no header the site does not know who is asking
issues.text: RFC 9110 §15.5.2: "The server generating a 401 response MUST send a WWW-Authenticate header field ... containing at least one challenge applicable to the target resource." The lab's /admin answers 401 from a bare Caddy `respond` with no such header, so the run the lesson presents as the picture of a 401 is one no conforming server may send. Nothing in the text is false — claim 8 states only what 401 means — but nothing marks the example as a stand-in either.
issues.fix: Leave the lesson body alone (WWW-Authenticate is out of scope at L1) and add to depth_notes of this lesson in content/tracks/foundation/track.yaml: "Không dạy WWW-Authenticate / khung xác thực HTTP; 401 của lab dùng cookie nên không kèm challenge."

issues.quote: reason phrase — the short text after the number on the response's first line, its status line
issues.text: Stated for HTTP as such, but it is true only of HTTP/1.1 and earlier. RFC 9110 §6.2: "In HTTP/1.1 ... and earlier, control data is sent as the first line of a message. In HTTP/2 ... and HTTP/3 ..., control data is sent as pseudo-header fields" — no first line and no reason phrase there. Claim 11 was written with the HTTP/1.1 restriction; the Core concepts entry was not.
issues.fix: Write "the short text after the number on the first line of an HTTP/1.1 response, its status line", matching the `HTTP/1.1 302 Found` the run prints. No change to content/versions.yaml is needed: §15.1 and §6.2 of the pinned RFC 9110 already source claim 11.

issues.quote: proxy — a program standing between the client and the real server, taking the request and passing it on.
issues.text: The outline entry sets `vocab: []`, yet section 3 introduces four terms — status class, reason phrase, redirection, proxy. "proxy" does not appear anywhere in content/glossary.yaml, and it then carries weight in the last paragraph of section 5, in summary line 4 and in quiz q7. Under CLAUDE.md rule 2 a term used this way belongs in the lesson's vocab.
issues.fix: Owner only. Add `proxy` (and, if it is to stay a defined term, `reason phrase`) to `vocab` for foundation.l1.http-status-codes in content/tracks/foundation/track.yaml and to glossary.yaml through tools/merge-outline. Do not change the lesson text.

issues.quote: A 5xx from a proxy (502/503) usually means the app behind it is down or slow, not that the proxy is broken.
issues.text: The outline entry is wrong about 503 and the lesson is right to depart from it. RFC 9110 §15.6.4 defines 503 with no intermediary — "a temporary overload or scheduled maintenance" — and the lab's own 503 for /slow comes from Caddy, which has nothing behind it at stage-0. Item 4 is therefore only half established by the lesson, and leaving the outline as written invites a regeneration to reintroduce the error.
issues.fix: Owner only. Edit content/tracks/foundation/track.yaml, outline item 4 of foundation.l1.http-status-codes, to: "A 502 comes from a server acting as a gateway and points at the server behind it; a 503 can come from any server, including the proxy itself." Do not change the lesson text, which is already correct.

beyond_scope: Section 4 teaches the RFC 9110 rule that an unrecognised code is treated as the x00 of its class, and quiz q3 tests it. Not an outline item, but it is what makes "the digit, not the exact number, is the contract" true rather than a slogan; keep it and add it to the outline.

Outline item 4 is only half established: 502 as written, while the 503 half of the item is deliberately (and correctly) contradicted — see the scope issue, which is an owner edit to track.yaml, not a lesson fix. Items 1, 2 and 3 are fully established and the codes taught are exactly item 2's list; depth_notes are respected (no full status table, no RFC 9457).

issues.quote: `/api/v1/orders/999` answers `404`, and so does `/no-such-page` … yet no two of those answers mean the same thing.
issues.text: The same sentence tells me two addresses both answer `404`, and then the next clause says no two answers mean the same thing. I stopped and counted: two of the seven are the same number. Section 5 later says both `404`s say the same thing (the server has nothing here) and only the cause differs, and quiz q4 is built on exactly that. So the opening claim reads as wrong on my first pass, and I could not tell whether the lesson wanted me to see the two `404`s as different or as identical.
issues.fix: Replace "yet no two of those answers mean the same thing" with a sentence that admits the repeat, e.g. "yet those numbers do not all mean the same thing, and the two that share a number did not get there the same way."

issues.quote: The first digit is the status class, the part every client must understand: `2xx` the request succeeded
issues.text: The whole section is written in `2xx` / `3xx` / `x00` notation, but nothing says what the letters stand for. I guessed that `2xx` means "any code whose first digit is 2" from the surrounding sentence, and `x00` from the list `200`, `300`, `400`, `500` that follows it. The guess worked, but it was a guess, and the summary uses the same notation.
issues.fix: After "The first digit is the status class", add one clause spelling the notation out: "written `2xx`, `3xx`, `4xx`, `5xx`, where the x's stand for any two digits".

issues.quote: `304` says nothing has changed, so reuse the copy you already hold and read no body.
issues.text: This assumes I am already holding a copy of something. Nothing before this point says a client keeps an earlier answer, so I could not picture when a `304` would be useful, and "read no body" left me wondering what I would show instead. The diagram's 3xx branch has the same half ("or you already hold what you need"), so I could not narrate that arrow either.
issues.fix: In the `3xx` paragraph, after "reuse the copy you already hold", add "if you kept one from an earlier answer", and keep the Connections pointer to the caching lesson.

issues.quote: `502` a proxy — a server acting as a gateway — got an unusable answer from the server behind it
issues.text: "gateway" is a new word to me. Core concepts told me a proxy is a program standing between the client and the real server; here the same thing is renamed "a server acting as a gateway", and summary line 4 drops the word "proxy" entirely and keeps only "gateway". I had to decide on my own that the two names are one thing.
issues.fix: Use the Core concepts wording in both places: "a proxy, the program standing between you and the real server, got an unusable answer from the server behind it", and start summary line 4 with "`502` comes from a proxy".

issues.quote: redirection — an answer that does not carry what you asked for
issues.text: "redirection" is defined in Core concepts and then never appears again anywhere in the lesson. The `3xx` paragraph, the diagram and the run all describe the behaviour in other words, so I finished the lesson unsure whether `302` is what that term was naming.
issues.fix: Use the word once where it belongs: open the `3xx` paragraph with "Within `3xx`, the redirections: `301` says the address has moved for good …".

issues.text: `localhost` appears in every command in the block and in the prose walk-through, but nothing says what it names. I know what a port is and what an IP address is, so `:8080` was fine; I could not tell whether `localhost` is a name the lab set up, something DNS resolves, or a fixed word every machine understands.

issues.text: I had to re-read this sentence three times. It carries the point (nothing answered, so there is no number), but in the middle it explains `set -euo pipefail`, "a test", and the `||` on line 5 — none of which the lesson taught me — and by the end I had lost the subject of the sentence.

issues.quote: Read the seven numbers as classes first: one `2xx`, one `3xx`, four `4xx`, one `5xx`;
issues.text: This one paragraph makes five separate points: the classes in the run, the reason phrase, the two `404`s, the `401`/`403` pair, and the rule that a server may answer `404` where `403` would be true. I re-read it twice to work out which sentence answered which of my questions.
